operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Yitro 7:1: “In truth, the blessed God cannot be grasped at all, and the description ‘holy’ does not apply to Him except because Israel recognizes His holiness. This is what is called apprehending Him: that He is holy, separate from every apprehension. Through this, the blessed God is called holy. This is why, concerning God’s holiness, he brought the verse, ‘You are holy, enthroned upon the praises of Israel’: through Israel’s praises, the blessed God is called holy, because they recognize His holiness and kingship.”

anchor.hebrewAnchor: שֶׁעַל יְדֵי קְדוּשַׁתְכֶם אֲנִי קָדוֹשׁ מִלְּמַעְלָה.

operations.text: Tzidkat HaTzadik 261:1: “The Holy One, blessed be He—His glory fills the whole earth, and no place is empty of Him. Yet He is greatly concealed: ‘He makes darkness His hiding place.’ When this recognition illuminates a person’s heart—how the blessed God’s glory fills the whole earth—this is called ‘He brought us from darkness to great light,’ as stated in the Haggadah. The Exodus from Egypt is the passage from the concealment of the recognition of the blessed God into its revelation. It is an illumination both for the person and for the blessed God, as our Sages said at the end of Bereishit Rabbah, chapter 30: a parable of a king walking through dark alleyways, whose friend came and lit a lamp. Abraham our father, peace be upon him, illuminated before the blessed God. For this is called the Divine Presence in exile: when His Presence among the lower beings is profoundly concealed and is neither revealed nor publicly known, it is like walking through dark alleyways.”

anchor.hebrewAnchor: דְּזֶה נִקְרָא שֶׁמֵּאִיר לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ,

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Shemot 3:1: “The matter is this: throughout the account of Creation it is written, ‘God saw that it was good.’ How can the expression ‘He saw’ apply? Had He not seen creation beforehand? Rather, the meaning is that through the blessed God’s seeing creation and looking upon it, He placed within it the light that is good.”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Shemot 3: ‘Expounds ‘And she saw him that he was good’ (Exodus 2:2)—how the divine light hidden in Moses shone forth at his birth.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 13:2: “The verse ‘A nation and a congregation of nations,’ which they interpreted concerning Elijah’s deed on Mount Carmel, was said to Jacob our father, peace be upon him, before Benjamin’s birth, because Elijah came from Benjamin, as stated at the end of Bereishit Rabbah, chapter 71. Although some say that he came from Gad, as stated there, and some say that he was a priest, as in Bava Metzia 114b and Tosafot there, all are true: he comprises many souls, as is known from the words of the Arizal. Here the root of his soul that comes from Benjamin is indicated.”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 13: ‘Expounds the Arizal's teaching that the soul of a leader of Israel encompasses the root-sparks of the entire generation.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Vayechi 13:1: “He said this concerning the tribe of Asher in accordance with what I heard from our holy master, of blessed memory. He said that Amos, who was of the tribe of Asher and came from Tekoa, spoke the passage ‘Are you not like the children of Cush?’ It is founded upon the cry of young people, for one who has blemished the covenant is called disfigured and Cushite—the opposite of Joseph, who is called ‘handsome in form and handsome in appearance.’ This is because that blemish is more common in this tribe. Thus far his words. The meaning is that this tribe was given an especially great power to repair the serpent’s blemish and corruption. Its root was in eating; subsequently it extended to his coming upon Eve and imparting impurity to her, from which the corruption of the hundred and thirty years extended.”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Vayechi 13: ‘Expounds the perfection of Joseph the Tzaddik (‘handsome in form and handsome in appearance,’ Genesis 39:6), whose body and covenant remained wholly unblemished.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Shemot 8:1: “Afterward the holy Zohar says: ‘Great is crying out, for it rules in this world and the World to Come; through crying out a person inherits this world and the World to Come,’ as it is written, ‘They cried out to the Lord,’ and so forth. Its proof is that the passage begins, ‘Let the redeemed of the Lord say so.’ This refers to the World to Come: Binah, the world that is coming. For when a person takes to heart that the supreme King of kings stands over him, awe reaches him. This is ‘The beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord’; the Shabbat of Friday evening ‘is awe, and awe rests within it’ (Zohar I, 5b). The lower Divine Presence is also called the heart, as ‘but he has no heart’ is interpreted in Yoma 72b concerning one who lacks fear of Heaven. Through awe one comes to repentance: the expression ‘awe’ is interpreted as repentance in Avodah Zarah 19a and Berakhot 17a, for through awe a person remembers his sins, regrets them and repents of them. When awe enters the depths of the heart, ‘His heart will understand, and he will return’—this is Binah, the heart. Thus, ‘it rules in this world’ means awe, which is the attribute of Malchut; ‘and in the World to Come’ means repentance, Binah, the world that is coming.”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Shemot 10: ‘Expounds the power of Israel's heartfelt cry (tze'akah) in Egypt, through which a person inherits both this world and the World to Come.’

operations.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Bereshit 7:1: “The Holy One, blessed be He, who is called righteous and upright, created the human being in His image only so that he would be righteous and upright like Him. If you ask, ‘Why did He create the evil inclination, of which it is written, “The inclination of the human heart is evil from youth” (Genesis 8:21)? You say that it is evil—who can make it good?’ the Holy One, blessed be He, says: ‘You make it evil.’ Why? A child of five, six, seven, eight or nine does not sin; rather, from ten onward, he then develops the evil inclination.”
operations.beforeText: Midrash Tanchuma, Bereshit 7:1: ‘Midrash Tanchuma, Bereshit 7: Expounds how Hashem created the evil inclination only so that man might conquer and sweeten it through the light of the Torah, turning darkness into light.’

operations.text: Zohar, Pinchas 53:332: “For this reason the masters of the Mishnah established: ‘Study is not the essential thing, but action.’ For the Holy One, blessed be He, is concealed in the mysteries of Torah. Through what is He known? Through the commandments, which are His Divine Presence, which is His likeness. Just as He is humble, His Divine Presence is humility. He is pious, and she is pious; He is mighty, and she is sovereign over all the nations of the world. He is truth, and she is faith.”
operations.beforeText: Zohar, Pinchas 53:332: ‘Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 1: Expounds Sefer Yetzirah 5:10 on the letter Tzadi, the month of Shevat, and the tribe of Asher (‘Out of Asher his bread shall be fat,’ Genesis 49:20) in rectifying the holiness of eating and the covenant.’

operations.text: Zohar, Pinchas 123:841: “The first commandment is called “Anokhi” from the side of Keter, which is ayin, “Nothingness,” from our God. Anokhi contains kaf—Keter—and contains ayin.”
operations.beforeText: Zohar, Pinchas 123:841: ‘Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 1: Expounds Sefer Yetzirah 5:10 on the letter Tzadi, the month of Shevat, and the tribe of Asher (‘Out of Asher his bread shall be fat,’ Genesis 49:20) in rectifying the holiness of eating and the covenant.’

operations.text: Tikkunei Zohar 11b:6: “When she is taken from Chesed, she is called the Written Torah, given from the right, as it is written, ‘From His right hand, a fiery law for them.’ When she is taken from Gevurah, she is called the Oral Torah, for thus the masters of the Mishnah established: ‘The Oral Torah was given from the mouth of Gevurah.’ From there come the mighty who stand in the breach. Only one who is mighty in the battle of Torah, mighty over his inclination, can stand within her.”
operations.beforeText: Tikkunei Zohar 11b:6: ‘Tikkunei Zohar, Introduction (11b): Expounds the correspondence between the Ten Commandments and the ten utterances of Creation, linking the fourth commandment (Shabbat) with the supernal rest of Binah and Malchut.’

operations.text: Zohar, Eikev 1:18: “Meanwhile an elder appeared before him and said: ‘Faithful Shepherd, prepare a table for your Master, for Him and for the Matron, with every kind of delight, to fulfill thereby, “This is the table that is before the Lord” (Ezekiel 41:22). Until now, all have delighted in the King’s table, as it is written, “Come, eat of My bread” (Proverbs 9:5). This is the bread of the Written Torah and the wine of the Oral Torah. There are many delicacies there—kinds of Torah’s meanings—sweeter than all the foods and delights of the world and of the king.’”

operations.text: Zohar, Pinchas 73:453: “Rabbi Shimon opened and said: “Hear, Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). The ayin is enlarged, and so too the dalet. Together they form the sign ed, “witness,” as it is written, “The Lord is witness among you” (I Samuel 12:5). The letters shin and mem remain—the mem is open. Why is it not closed? Because the closed mem is the upper King (another reading: the upper world); the open mem is the lower King (another reading: the lower world).”
operations.beforeText: Zohar, Pinchas 73:453: ‘Zohar, Pinchas (III:236b): Expounds how the letters Alef and Tav illuminate the letter Mem (Malchut), forming Emet (Truth) and uniting the beginning and end of thought in action.’

operations.text: Zohar, Sh'lach 30:231: “He said to him: ‘The air of the Garden of Eden is the breathing of the holy spirit, and the righteous clothe themselves in it, as they were in this world. Afterward, the holy spirit rests upon the head of each one; it is crowned and becomes a crown for him. So it was with Mordecai: it is written, “In royal clothing”—the likeness of that world—and afterward, “And a great crown of gold.” This is the crown that rests upon the heads of the righteous in that world.’”
operations.beforeText: Zohar, Sh'lach 30:230-231: ‘Zohar, Sh'lach (III:169b): Expounds the supernal garments of royal blue and white worn by Mordecai (Esther 8:15) as the garments of the soul woven from Torah and mitzvot.’

operations.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Devarim 2:1: “At the end of forty years after Israel left Egypt, he began explaining the Torah in seventy languages, as it is said, ‘He explained this Torah.’ The mouth that had said, ‘I am not a man of words,’ said, ‘These are the words.’ And the prophet cried out and said, ‘Then the lame will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will sing’ (Isaiah 35:6). Why? ‘For waters will burst forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.’ Therefore it is said, ‘These are the words.’”
operations.beforeText: Midrash Tanchuma, Devarim 2: ‘Expounds Moses' repetition and explanation of the Torah (Mishneh Torah) in the eleventh month (Shevat), opening the gates of the Oral Torah for all generations.’

operations.text: Zohar, Nasso 4:49: “Hei never rests within a person, nor does Vav, without awe and without love, which are Yod-Hei: we indeed call them awe and love. From there were given the Torah and the commandment, which are son and daughter. Because Israel fulfills the Torah and the commandment, they are called children of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written, ‘You are children of the Lord your God’ (Deuteronomy 14:1).”

operations.text: Chiddushei Ramban on Bava Batra 12a:1: “Rather, this is what it says: although the prophecy of the prophets—which consists of revelation and vision—was taken away, the prophecy of the sages, which comes through wisdom, was not taken away. Rather, they know the truth through the holy spirit within them.”
operations.beforeText: Chiddushei Ramban on Bava Batra 12a:1: ‘Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 1: Expounds Sefer Yetzirah 5:10 on the letter Tzadi, the month of Shevat, and the tribe of Asher (‘Out of Asher his bread shall be fat,’ Genesis 49:20) in rectifying the holiness of eating and the covenant.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Vaera 7:1: “In truth, there is a difference: at first he said, ‘I am not a man of words.’ Moses our teacher is called ‘the man of God,’ the husband of the Matron, as stated in the holy Zohar (22b): ‘Master of the house—the man of God.’ This is ‘a man of words,’ in accordance with the holy Zohar (I, 32a): ‘This speech is called Shabbat, for Shabbat is called speech.’ Concerning this he said, ‘I am not a man of words,’ because speech was in exile.”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Vaera 7: ‘Expounds the exile of speech (galut ha-dibur) in Egypt—why Moses said ‘I am not a man of words’ (Exodus 4:10)—and how the redemption of speech is the revelation of the Oral Torah.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 1:1: “‘He made the letter tzadi rule over swallowing’: the serpent’s first enticement concerned eating, to feel bodily pleasure in it. From this came the serpent’s approaching Eve and imparting impurity to her, as stated in the Gemara (Shabbat 146a), and from this extended the hundred and thirty years, for Adam became one whose foreskin was drawn forward, as stated in Sanhedrin 38b. The work of this month is to introduce holiness into eating, as it is written, ‘The righteous person eats to satisfy his soul.’ This follows Rambam’s words in chapter 3 of Hilkhot De‘ot: if one eats in order to have strength to serve God and sleeps so that his mind will rest, his eating and sleeping are found to be service of the blessed Omnipresent.”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 1: ‘Expounds Sefer Yetzirah 5:10 on the letter Tzadi, the month of Shevat, and the tribe of Asher (‘Out of Asher his bread shall be fat,’ Genesis 49:20) in rectifying the holiness of eating and the covenant.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 1:1: “In Sefer Yetzirah: ‘He made the letter tzadi rule over swallowing … and Shevat in the year, and the gizzard in the person.’ This follows what is stated in Berakhot 61b: ‘The gizzard grinds.’ Concerning the letter tzadi, Shabbat 104a says: ‘A bent tzadi and a straight tzadi: a bent righteous person and a straight righteous person.’ One who guards the covenant is called righteous, as stated in the holy Zohar (II, 23a). That is, the ninth attribute is ‘the righteous one, foundation of the world’; its completeness is when it includes all ten attributes, and nine times ten equals ninety, tzadi.”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 1: ‘Expounds Sefer Yetzirah 5:10 on the letter Tzadi, the month of Shevat, and the tribe of Asher (‘Out of Asher his bread shall be fat,’ Genesis 49:20) in rectifying the holiness of eating and the covenant.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2:4: “Joshua was the first to write his own book after the Five Books of the Torah, and it is a form of Oral Torah. This is what is said in Nedarim 22b: ‘Had Israel not sinned, only the Five Books of the Torah and the book of Joshua would have been given to them, for it contains the arrangement of the Land of Israel.’ The Land of Israel is called the inheritance of the Lord; it is the root of ‘land,’ which is the attribute of Malchut, the mouth, the Oral Torah. The book of Joshua is the portion of Oral Torah that every soul of Israel has in Torah; each person’s portion in the Land of Israel points to it.”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2: ‘Expounds the victory of the Hasmonean priests and the illumination of the Oral Torah in the darkness of exile.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 4:1: “They interpret ‘He made the letter tzadi rule over thought’ as follows: tzadi alludes to the righteous person, who is ‘mighty, subduing his inclination.’ This means that he still has work and struggle with the evil inclination and still needs light—that the blessed God illuminate him so that he can overcome it. As we have often said concerning ‘The righteous are destined for light’ (Ta‘anit 15a), for it is written, ‘Light is sown for the righteous.’ This is through the light of Torah, as stated in the holy Zohar (I, 202a): ‘There is nothing that breaks the evil inclination except Torah.’ Through thinking about Torah one is saved from foolish thoughts.”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 4: ‘Expounds the gizzard that grinds (Berakhot 61b) and the letter Tzadi in Sefer Yetzirah as refining thought and appetite through the toil of Torah.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 3:1: “Concerning Jacob our father, peace be upon him, it is written, ‘And He will give me bread to eat and clothing to wear.’ Why does it say ‘to eat’ and ‘to wear’? Who does not know that bread is for eating and clothing is for wearing? Concerning the convert, where it is written, ‘To give him bread and clothing,’ it does not say ‘bread to eat and clothing to wear.’ Rather, Jacob our father asked that the blessed God give him the bread and also the eating—that He feed him, and the eating be in holiness. Likewise, He should give him the clothing and the wearing—that the blessed God clothe him.”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 3: ‘Expounds how holy eating is sustained directly by Hashem, transforming physical food into spiritual vitality.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 4:1: “This is what is said, ‘He gives food to those who fear Him,’ and likewise, ‘She gives food to her household’: those who fear Him eat only like a wolf taking its prey, without bodily self-gratification. Their eating is solely to sustain life, for the blessed God created the human being to need to take food into himself to sustain life, and His will is fulfilled thereby. This is ‘She gives food to her household’: the Torah scholars, who are the members of the household of the Congregation of Israel, as is known.”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 4: ‘Expounds the gizzard that grinds (Berakhot 61b) and the letter Tzadi in Sefer Yetzirah as refining thought and appetite through the toil of Torah.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 2:1: “The letter yud signifies the covenant, as stated in the holy Zohar (II, 36a): ‘Because yud is revealed,’ and so forth; see there. Likewise, the Midrash (Tanchuma, Tazria 5) says: ‘What is the Name and seal He placed upon them? It is Shaddai: shin in the nose, dalet in the hand, and yud in circumcision.’ The Name Shaddai is the ninth Name, corresponding to the attribute ‘the righteous one, foundation of the world,’ as stated in Zohar III, 11b.”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 2: ‘Expounds the bent Tzadi and straight Tzadi (Shabbat 104a) as the work of humbling and sanctifying physical desire in the month of Shevat.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Vaera 7:1: “In Sefer Yetzirah it is stated: ‘Shabbat in the year, and the mouth in the person.’ The holy Zohar (III, 201b) says: ‘When the day is sanctified, the mouth that rules over all ascends—the mouth of the Lord.’ We have said that the human mouth certainly was not created on Shabbat, for Adam spoke on Friday. Rather, ‘the mouth of the Lord’ means that a person speaks and it is the word of the Lord—‘My words which I have placed in your mouth.’ This was created on Shabbat, when the day was sanctified. This is ‘Malchut is the mouth; we call it the Oral Torah.’”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Vaera 7: ‘Expounds the exile of speech (galut ha-dibur) in Egypt—why Moses said ‘I am not a man of words’ (Exodus 4:10)—and how the redemption of speech is the revelation of the Oral Torah.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2:3: “We find in many places ‘a law given to Moses at Sinai.’ Since it is said to be from Sinai, why was it not written? We have explained that this is Moses our teacher’s Oral Torah: the blessed God illuminated Moses’s mind, and he originated these laws through his reasoning. Concerning this, Nedarim 38a says, ‘Rather, the power of analysis alone’—this the blessed God entrusted only to Moses. It is called ‘a law given to Moses at Sinai’ because Moses knew explicitly that these laws were from Sinai, just like the entire Written Torah. Moses transmitted them to Israel as laws without their reasons. No person can arrive at their reasons through prophecy except Moses, of whom it is written, ‘No prophet has arisen again,’ and so forth. Only through the aspect of the holy spirit was prophecy not taken from the sages: a sage originates something through his understanding, and a law given to Moses at Sinai is found to agree with him.”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2: ‘Expounds the victory of the Hasmonean priests and the illumination of the Oral Torah in the darkness of exile.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Bo 4:1: “This accords with what was said (Eruvin 21b): “The mandrakes have given fragrance”—these are the young men of Israel who have not tasted sin. We have already said that the expression “young men of Israel” indicates that “sin” here means a blemish of the covenant, to which youth and early life give rise. Since they have not tasted this sin, they give a good fragrance. Conversely, one who causes such a blemish, Heaven forbid, has a repulsive odor. Hence the inclination toward desire is called “this repulsive one,” for it is repellent and repulsive, as was said (Shabbat 151a), “A woman is a skin-bottle,” etc. Concerning this they said (Sukkah 52b): “If this repulsive one encounters you, draw him to the study hall”—draw the desire so that it becomes delight in the teaching and love of Torah, as it will be in the future, as stated in Midrash HaNe’elam (Zohar I, 138a).”

anchor.hebrewAnchor: וְעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר עַל הַטְּהוֹרִים מִפְּגָם זֶה: "הַדּוּדָאִים נָתְנוּ רֵיחַ".

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Ki Teitzei 1:1: “The principal remedy is the Oral Torah, which comes to repair the abundance of vexation, as it is said, “For with much wisdom comes much vexation.” This is the meaning of “draw him to the study hall”: a study hall is the place where people expound and originate new Torah teachings, which is Oral Torah. This is a remedy for the evil inclination, to repair “the fool’s heart at his left.” As stated in the holy Zohar: “There is nothing that breaks the evil inclination except Torah.””

anchor.hebrewAnchor: מְקוֹם חִדּוּשׁ הֲלָכוֹת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה.

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Vayetzei 3:3: “In the Rav’s Siddur, on the verse “From new moon to its new moon,” he asks why it says “its new moon.” We may say that a month is named for renewal. Thus “its new moon” hints that each Rosh Chodesh has a different renewal: each of the twelve months of the year has its own arrangement of the letters of the divine Name, its own one of the twelve simple letters, and its own bodily organ, as stated in Sefer Yetzirah. Likewise, in every year each Rosh Chodesh has a new renewal. “From Sabbath to its Sabbath” also hints at this: each Sabbath has a fresh renewal of holiness. Hence it is called a bride each and every Sabbath. A woman is a bride only once, during the seven days of celebration; but every Sabbath has a different, newly shining holiness.”

anchor.hebrewAnchor: שֶׁבְּכָל חֹדֶשׁ מִתְחַדֵּשׁ עִנְיָן מְחֻדָּשׁ בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה וְכֵן בְּכָל שַׁבָּת וְשַׁבָּת;

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Chayei Sara 1:2: “There is an evil inclination of desire that is called fire. Likewise, the inclination of jealousy and honor is also called fire, as explained in Vayera, teaching 1, beginning “And also.” There is also the shell of Amalek, of whom it says, “who cooled you”—who chilled and cooled you. This means that he casts coldness and laziness upon a person. This is the first of the shells, and it assails even great people. Thus concerning Jabez they interpreted “that it not cause me pain” (Temurah 16a): “that the evil inclination not prevent me from studying.” The root of the serpent and the evil inclination is called sadness, for it brought sadness and toil into the world. This is “She does not fear snow for her household.” Not only does she not fear the fire of desire, jealousy, and honor—the three kinds of fire—but she does not even fear snow, the first of the shells, which casts laziness and coldness. “She does not fear for her household” means the great people who are called her household. Why? “For all her household are clothed in two”—Sabbath and circumcision, both of which indicate that they are attached at the root to the utterance “In the beginning,” the beginning of holiness.”

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Lech Lecha 4:1: “Likewise, regarding Abraham’s feast, Tosafot (Shabbat 130a) cites Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer: “On the day heh-gimel [five plus three], he circumcised”—the eighth day of circumcision. Isaac was the first to be circumcised on the eighth day. Since an infant is circumcised on the eighth day without his own understanding and thereby becomes an Israelite, this indicates that he is attached at the root, in the beginning of divine thought.”

anchor.hebrewAnchor: וְהַיְנוּ שֶׁנּוֹלַד מִתּוֹלָדָה יִשְׂרָאֵל.

operations.text: Eikhah Rabbah 2:3: “Another interpretation: “He did not remember His footstool.” This footstool is none other than the Temple, as it is written: “Exalt the Lord our God, and bow down at His footstool; He is holy.””
operations.beforeText: Eikhah Rabbah 5:21: ‘Turn us unto You, O Lord, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old’ (Lamentations 5:21): the Midrash expounds the enduring sanctity of the site of the Temple—‘the house of the footstool of our God’—where the Divine Presence never departs from the Western Wall and the foundation of the Sanctuary.’

operations.text: Moed Katan 16b:21: “Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: What is the meaning of “The utterance of David son of Jesse, the utterance of the man raised on high”? It is the utterance of David son of Jesse, who established the yoke of repentance.”
operations.beforeText: Moed Katan 16b: “Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: What is meant by ‘The utterance of David son of Yishai, and the utterance of the man who was raised on high’? It is the utterance of David son of Yishai, who established the yoke of repentance.”

operations.text: Ramban on Exodus 3:18:1: “In Shemot Rabbah (3:8): “Immediately, they will listen to your voice.” Why? Because they possess a tradition of redemption: any redeemer who comes and says the doubled expression of remembrance is a true redeemer. This is the wording of that aggadah. You may ask: How do they know to believe him? Perhaps Moses heard this tradition just as they did. One may answer that this is what they received from Joseph, who heard it from his father the prophet: the first person who comes and speaks to them in this wording will be the one to redeem them. It was revealed and known before the Holy One, blessed be He, that no one would come and deceive them; with this He assured them.”

operations.text: Ramban on Genesis 49:10:1: “This was the punishment of the Hasmoneans who reigned during the Second Temple. They were supremely pious, and without them the Torah and the commandments would have been forgotten in Israel. Nevertheless, they were severely punished: the four pious sons of the elder Hasmonean who reigned one after another, despite all their strength and success, fell by the sword into the hands of their enemies. The punishment ultimately reached the point described by our Sages: “Anyone who says, ‘I descend from the house of the Hasmoneans,’ is a slave,” for they were all cut off because of this sin. Although the descendants of Shimon suffered punishment because of the Sadducees, all the descendants of the righteous Matityahu the Hasmonean perished only because they reigned without belonging to the tribe of Judah or the house of David, completely removing the scepter and the ruler’s staff. operations.beforeText: Zohar, Pinchas 245a: ‘In the Zohar (Pinchas, Ra’aya Meheimna III 245a), the controversies between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel are rooted in the supernal pillars: Beit Hillel derives from Chesed (the Right Side of Abraham, which is fitting for the present world of construction), whereas Beit Shammai derives from Gevurah and fierce exactitude (the Left Side of Isaac), whose sublime light will become the practiced halakhah in the World to Come.’

operations.text: Zohar, Vayeshev 16:157 (printed gloss; I, 186b): ““River” alludes to the holy covenant impressed in his flesh, which is the likeness of that river: the mystery of the righteous one, who is joined with righteousness as one above. operations.beforeText: Zohar, Tetzaveh 14:127-16:138: ‘In the Zohar (Tetzaveh II 186b), the verse ‘Honor and majesty (Hod ve-Hadar) are before Him’ (Psalms 96:6) is expounded: ‘Who is Hadar (Majesty / Beauty)? operations.beforeText: Zohar, Vayeshev 190a: ‘In the Zohar (Vayeshev I 190a), Rabbi Abba teaches: ‘When a person sees unholy thoughts or the enticements of the Evil Inclination approaching him, let him immediately engage in words of Torah, and they will vanish from before him—for there is no weapon that shatters the Evil Inclination other than the Torah.’’

operations.text: Turei Zahav on Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 670:3: “The Levush made a distinction, saying that on Purim lives were saved, whereas on Chanukah lives were not saved, because the Greeks did not seek their lives but only their subjugation and abandonment of their religion. operations.beforeText: Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 670:2: ‘Taz (Orach Chayim 670:3, citing the Levush) explains why Purim has an obligation of festive meals (mishteh ve-simchah) whereas Chanukah’s primary obligation is Hallel and praise rather than feasting: on Purim Haman decreed to annihilate the physical bodies of Israel, so the salvation is celebrated with bodily feasting; on Chanukah the Greeks sought to uproot the soul and the Torah while leaving the body intact if Israel assimilated, so the salvation is celebrated through spiritual praise and the light of Torah.’

operations.text: Zohar, Bereshit 35:339: “The verse specifies these six supernal days: “Yours, Lord, are greatness, might, beauty…” “For all”—this is the righteous one. “In heaven”—this is Tiferet. “And on earth”—this is the Congregation of Israel. operations.beforeText: Zohar, Bereshit 35:339-36:352: ‘In the Zohar (Bereshit I 31a–31b), the attribute of Tzaddik Yesod Olam (embodied in Joseph) is expounded on the verse ‘For all that is in the heaven and in the earth’ (I Chronicles 29:11): Yesod is the covenantal bond that unites Heaven (Tiferet, the Holy One, blessed be He) and Earth (Malkhut, the Shekhinah).’

operations.text: Zohar, Sh'lach 10:65: “Furthermore: “Amalek dwells in the land of the south.” If a person says that, despite all this, he will attain it—“Amalek dwells in the land of the south”: this is the evil inclination, the accuser who accuses a person and is continually present in the body.”
operations.beforeText: Zohar, Sh'lach 9:59-10:67: ‘In the Zohar (Sh’lach III 160a), Amalek is identified as the inner evil inclination and spiritual prosecutor (mekatreg) that continually lurks within a person to cool his enthusiasm in serving Hashem whenever his hands weaken from the toil of Torah.’

operations.text: Zohar, Pinchas 126:877: “The tefillin of the Master of the world are Keter. What is the crown of the Master of the world? YHWH: yud is Chochmah; heh is Binah; vav is Tiferet, encompassing six sefirot; heh is Malkhut.”
operations.beforeText: Zohar, Pinchas 124:867-127:879: ‘In the Zohar (Pinchas, Ra’aya Meheimna III 258a), the four letters of the Name Havayah are explained as embracing all the Sefirot: the upper tip of the Yud is Keter; Yud is Chokhmah; Hei is Binah; Vav encompasses the six attributes of Ze’ir Anpin (the Holy One, blessed be He); and the final Hei is Malkhut (His Shekhinah).’

operations.beforeText: Zohar, Terumah 2:12-4:23: ‘In the Zohar (Terumah II 127a, 180a), the four directions of the world and the vessels of the Tabernacle are aligned with the four camps of the Shekhinah and the Primordial Light that shines from East, South, North, and West.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Purim 2:3: ““And His Holy One into a flame”—this is Esther. This follows the statement in Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 21, that the Holy One, blessed be He, covered Esther with His sign, for she is His holiness. That is, Esther too was of the aspect of Joseph the righteous. As stated at the beginning of Midrash Rabbah on Kedoshim, wherever you find a boundary against sexual immorality, you find holiness: anyone who guards himself against sexual immorality is called holy. Thus the Gemara, Megillah 13a, says: Her name was Esther; why was she called Hadassah? After the righteous, who are called myrtles. The righteous are called myrtles because a myrtle gives a pleasant fragrance. Eruvin 21b states: “The mandrakes gave forth fragrance”—these are the young men of Israel who have not tasted sin. We have often explained that the expression “young men of Israel” appears to refer to the sin of damaging the covenant, to which youth gives rise, as explained concerning Rosh Chodesh Marcheshvan. A righteous person who is a vehicle for the quality “foundation of the world” is called a myrtle because he gives a pleasant fragrance. Since Esther was called Hadassah, it follows that she was righteous and holy, of the aspect of Joseph the righteous.”

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Pekudei 10:1: “As we have already said, a person is called one who journeys throughout his life, as it is said, “For the person journeys to his eternal home.” Every righteous person has a world of his own, as Midrash Rabbah, Pekudei 52, says: It does not say “worlds,” but “his world.” All the working days correspond to “When the Ark journeyed … may Your enemies scatter and those who hate You flee.” Then a person journeys from stage to stage. When Shabbat comes, it is “When it rested, he would say: Return, O Lord.” The holiness of Shabbat always accords with the holiness of the labor of the working days; thus the six working days are always mentioned before Shabbat, as explained in Kedushat Shabbat 1 and elsewhere. On Shabbat, holiness then shines into the working days that follow, and they possess greater holiness than the preceding six working days. When the second Shabbat arrives, it gains further holiness; it likewise bestows greater holiness on the coming working days. So it continues forever: throughout his life, the person journeys.”

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Korach 8:4: “We find in the Talmud, Bava Batra 172a and elsewhere, the case of two people living in one town, each named Joseph son of Simeon. It would seemingly have been more fitting to use the example Reuben son of Jacob; why specifically Joseph son of Simeon? We have explained that all Israel are called by Joseph’s name, as it is said, “The remnant of Joseph,” and as stated in Bereshit Rabbah 71. This accords with “Your people are all righteous,” and with the statement of the holy Zohar, II, 23a: everyone who is circumcised is called righteous. Thus it uses Joseph son of Simeon as its example. Even though most of the twenty-four thousand who died over the matter of Peor were from the tribe of Simeon, which is the opposite of the quality of Joseph the righteous, in truth he too is called by Joseph’s name: the quality of the righteous person who guards the covenant. This is the meaning of Joseph son of Simeon.”

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Hashanah 5:1: “At the beginning of creation, the essence of life was words of Torah. Even eating, which sustains life, was also words of Torah, as it is said, “Come, eat of My bread and drink of the wine I have mixed,” interpreted in the holy Zohar, III, 271b, as the bread of the Written Torah and the wine of the Oral Torah. After the corruption that came through eating, when good and evil became mixed, nevertheless, when the festival of Rosh Hashanah arrives—the day of the world’s conception—one can also merit to taste only the good, as will be in the future. As I heard from our holy master of Ishbitz, of blessed memory, who said that in the future the verse will be joined as follows: “From every tree of the garden you may eat, and from the Tree of Knowledge of good”—you may also eat; “and evil you shall not eat.” Only the evil of the Tree of Knowledge shall you not eat. It will then become clear that Israel never ate anything but the good of the Tree of Knowledge. That is, the intention was solely words of Torah—Torah is light—and it is written, “God saw the light, that it was good.””

operations.text: Ketubot 2b:14-3a:1: “Rather, Rava stated his own reasoning: because of scrupulous women and because of unscrupulous women. operations.text: Zohar Chadash, Tikuna Kadma'ah 24: “For Adam sinned through the seven species: wheat, barley, grape, fig, pomegranate, oil-bearing olive, and honey. Therefore the Sages of the Mishnah said that the tree from which Adam ate was wheat; others said that it was a vine, and others said that it was a fig tree. operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Bo 2:2: “This is also alluded to in the verse, “So that you may recount in the ears of your son and your grandson.” It follows what I heard from the holy master, of blessed memory, who said that children are the depths of their father’s heart. Rabbi Menachem Azariah likewise wrote that the father’s soul is the son’s governing influence—that is, the root of life. This is the meaning of “So that you may recount”: through the locusts, they would attain the quality of understanding, the heart, and establish holiness for the generations—“So that you may recount.” In this He alluded to the plague of locusts, corresponding to understanding, the heart. Joel likewise says, “I will remove the northerner from you,” which in its plain meaning refers to the locusts. The Gemara, Sukkah 52a, says that Joel called it “the northerner,” and expounds: this is the evil inclination, which is hidden and stationed in a person’s heart. That is, in the hidden chambers of his heart. Thus the precise wording is “these signs of Mine within him.””

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2:3: “Although the Midrash, Rabbah and Tanchuma on Chukat, says, “His eye has seen every precious thing”—this refers to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues; matters not revealed to Moses were revealed to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues—and the Gemara there likewise says that Moses sat at the end of eight rows and did not understand what they were saying, nevertheless Rabbi Akiva did not apprehend the reason for a law given to Moses at Sinai, for that is Moses our teacher’s portion. Concerning this the Gemara says that Moses’s mind was put at ease: from this he saw that his understanding was higher, and that his portion of the Oral Torah was something no other person had attained. The portion of the Oral Torah belonging to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues does not pertain to Moses, because he had never brought about corruption and did not require the “abundant wisdom,” the fiftieth gate, entrusted to the penitent to repair the “abundant anger.””

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 5:1: “According to Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that the world was created in Tishrei, the order is that redemption will be in Tishrei: on Rosh Hashanah there will be an awakening to repentance through the sounding of the shofar, as it says, “If a shofar is sounded in a city, will the people not tremble?” Afterward comes Yom Kippur, to repair all that has passed; when they merit it, the union will then take place. Afterward comes Sukkot, the season of our rejoicing, and the war of Gog and Magog on Sukkot. Although through repentance the time of redemption is always available—as it says, “Today, if you heed His voice,” as stated in Sanhedrin 98a—at its appointed time the awakening to repentance will come from God, as it says, “I will remove the heart of stone,” and “I will bring it about that you follow My statutes.” According to Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds that the world was created in Nisan, the spirit of the Messiah was then created so that redemption would take place in Nisan when its appointed time arrived. Its order will resemble the redemption from Egypt, initiated by God: there will be plagues, Israel will be refined in all ten attributes, and redemption will come from God.”
operations.beforeText: Peri Tzadik, Bereshit 5: ‘Expounds why Bereishit immediately follows Simchat Torah and how Tishrei and Nisan represent the two complementary paths of awe and love.’

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 8:1: “From God’s side, the order is the quality of Abraham and afterward the quality of Isaac. The root of Abraham’s quality is love, as it says, “Abraham, who loved Me”; love brings eagerness in fulfilling positive commandments. Isaac’s quality, “the fear of Isaac,” is awe, which brings care in observing prohibitions, as we have explained from the Jerusalem Talmud, in Chayei Sarah, teaching 7. From God’s side, the order is “I am” and afterward “You shall have no other”: God bestows holiness and Torah upon “the wise person’s heart at his right,” and through this evil is uprooted from “the fool’s heart at his left.” As Shir HaShirim Rabbah, on “Let him kiss me,” states: when they heard the utterance “I am,” Torah study became fixed in their hearts; when they heard “You shall have no other,” the evil inclination was uprooted from their hearts. “I am” is the root of all positive commandments and Torah teachings, while “You shall have no other” is the root of the prohibitions. Thus, from God’s side, Abraham’s soul comes first and afterward Isaac’s; likewise, a heavenly voice proclaimed that the halakhah follows Beit Hillel, who belong to Abraham’s level. From the human side, however, the order is “Turn from evil” and afterward “Do good.” To attain Torah, awe must come first, enabling one to turn from evil; this is the quality of our father Isaac, peace be upon him. Thus Beit Shammai are always mentioned before Beit Hillel.”

operations.text: Peri Tzadik, Bo 7:1: “On Shabbat, a Jew attains these three forms of humility. “Poor” corresponds to “From where did you come? When he takes to heart that he will render an account before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, he becomes one who “trembles at My word.” For who can stand before His judgment, and who can be innocent before Him? He becomes utterly humble in his own eyes, is saved from all three kinds of husks, and can merit complete redemption.”
